name: Enterprise commerce architect
oneLine: Wants control, merchant-of-record status, customer data and predictable integration cost.
goals: Expose one commerce API (ACP, UCP, or both) that every agent surface can use, backed by the existing order management system.
Stay merchant of record: own the order, the tax calculation, the customer relationship and the first-party data.
Verify agent identity at the edge (TAP, Web Bot Auth) before the agent reaches catalog or checkout endpoints.
Accept agent-initiated payments through the existing PSP with the same tokenization and 3DS flows.
Keep a signed record of what the agent and the user authorized, for use in disputes.
Budget the integration once instead of chasing a new protocol every quarter.
pains: ACP, UCP, TAP and MPP each define their own headers, signing rules and discovery files, and vendors keep renaming fields.
Spec and schema drift (for example the ACP item quantity field) breaks integrations between dated versions.
Platform checkout can bypass merchant analytics pixels and loyalty logic, and the merchant loses the customer record.
RFC 9421 signing is required in several places but with different covered components and algorithms (Ed25519 in TAP samples, ES256 in UCP).
No liability shift exists for agent transactions, so a disputed agent order costs the merchant the same as any fraud case.
TAP terms are revocable and require full conformance within six months of any Visa change.
decisions: Which protocols to implement natively and which to reach through the PSP or a commerce platform.
Which agents to admit: only those verified by a key directory, only registered agents on a trusted list, or all signed traffic.
Where to enforce purchase limits and escalation: in the merchant API, in the PSP, or at the CDN.
Whether to require an AP2 mandate or Verifiable Intent before accepting an agent order.
How long to retain signatures, mandates and intent traces for dispute evidence.
